actions.justification: Mandatory first step — patient is tachycardic (HR 105) with hematemesis/melena; vital signs assessment is required to characterize hemodynamic status and severity of GI bleed.
Mandatory — patient with cirrhosis and active GI bleeding requires immediate hemodynamic assessment to determine shock index and guide resuscitation strategy.
Mandatory — large-bore IV access is critical in acute GI hemorrhage for fluid resuscitation and blood product administration.
MANDATORY: CBC is essential to assess hemoglobin/hematocrit levels and guide transfusion decisions in this patient with active upper GI bleeding.
MANDATORY: Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT) are critical in this cirrhotic patient who likely has coagulopathy contributing to bleeding risk.
MANDATORY: Type and crossmatch is required to prepare blood products for potential transfusion given active hematemesis and melena.

Cirrhotic patient with hematemesis has high likelihood of variceal bleeding. Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) reduces portal pressure and splanchnic blood flow, decreasing active variceal hemorrhage. Should be started immediately in suspected variceal bleeding per AASLD guidelines.

Upper GI bleeding requires urgent GI consultation for early endoscopy (within 12 hours per guidelines), which is both diagnostic and therapeutic, especially critical in a cirrhotic patient with likely variceal source.
BMP is essential to assess renal function (hepatorenal syndrome risk in cirrhosis), electrolytes, and glucose. These values guide resuscitation and help stratify bleeding severity and risk.
Assess tissue perfusion and severity of hemorrhagic shock in this tachycardic patient with active GI bleeding and cirrhosis.
Administer prokinetic agent (e.g., erythromycin) to promote gastric emptying and improve visualization at upcoming endoscopy, per UGIB guidelines.
IV proton pump inhibitor is indicated in upper GI bleeding to reduce rebleeding risk and as standard adjunctive therapy alongside octreotide.

Patient with cirrhosis and hematemesis/melena has ongoing GI bleed risk. Type and crossmatch is essential to prepare for potential blood transfusion. Although order_lab_type_and_crossmatch was done, this action ID is different and available in the current list.
HR 105 with hematemesis/melena indicates hemodynamic compromise. IV crystalloid bolus is indicated to support perfusion while awaiting blood products and further workup.
Initial lactate is pending but trending lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and severity of hemorrhagic shock in this patient with active GI bleed and tachycardia.

Initial CBC is pending; repeat CBC to trend hemoglobin and guide transfusion decisions in this cirrhotic patient with active GI bleeding (hematemesis/melena). Knowing the Hgb level is critical before deciding on packed RBC transfusion.

Patient with cirrhosis and active upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) with tachycardia (HR 105). Current guidelines recommend restrictive transfusion strategy with threshold of Hgb <7 g/dL in cirrhotic patients. Initiate transfusion protocol conditionally pending CBC result.
CT abdomen can help assess for portal hypertension complications, varices, and other sources of bleeding in this cirrhotic patient with hematemesis and melena, supporting pre-endoscopy workup.

Patient with cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena has initial CBC pending. Repeating CBC to trend hemoglobin and monitor for ongoing bleeding is essential in this GI hemorrhage patient who has already received blood products and resuscitation.

Patient with cirrhosis and active upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) with tachycardia may require surgical intervention if endoscopic or pharmacologic management fails. Early surgical consultation is warranted for bleeding preparedness.

Patient with cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena has received initial resuscitation, labs, and GI/surgery consults. Angiography may help identify and potentially treat the bleeding source (e.g., active variceal or non-variceal GI bleed) if endoscopic management is insufficient or to delineate vascular anatomy prior to intervention. This is the only available action and is clinically relevant for an upper GI bleed workup in a cirrhotic patient.

Cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding require prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) per guidelines to prevent bacterial infections including SBP and to reduce mortality - this has not been completed yet.

Upper endoscopy (EGD) should be performed within 12 hours of presentation for upper GI bleeding in cirrhosis to diagnose and treat variceal or non-variceal sources - preparation and scheduling is needed.
